topics.title: 1. OS Basics, Types & Distributed/Mobile Systems
topics.theory:
- **OS** = resource manager + virtual machine interface between user and hardware. **Functions:** process, memory, file, device/I-O management, security/protection, resource utilisation/accounting, user interface. MS-DOS, iOS, Linux are OSs; **LDAP is a protocol**, not an OS.
- **Types:** Batch, Multiprogramming, **Time-sharing (multitasking)**, **Real-time** (**hard** = strict deadlines e.g. flight control; **soft** = occasional misses OK), **Distributed** (many computers appear as one system; scalability, flexibility, resource sharing, fault tolerance), **Network OS** (shares files/resources across a network), Embedded, **Mobile OS** (Android, iOS, Symbian, Windows Mobile, Palm OS — "Manet OS" is not one).
- **Single-user single-tasking** systems (MS-DOS) need **no CPU scheduling**. OS/2 was a multitasking OS (IBM/Microsoft). Windows 3.x used non-preemptive (cooperative) multitasking; Unix/Linux are preemptive.
- **Abnormal termination = abort.** Program = passive entity; process = active entity. Cache/memory speed hierarchy: registers > cache > main memory > disk.
- **Distributed computing:** components shared among multiple computers working as one system; multiple machines provide the same service (fault tolerance); can add machines as required.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is/are a feature of distributed operating system? 

(i) Scalability 
(ii) Flexibility
qs.sol: A distributed operating system manages multiple networked computers and presents them as a coordinated system. Such systems are scalable because more machines can be added, and flexible because resources and services can be distributed or reconfigured. Therefore, both (i) and (ii) are correct, so option C is correct.
qs.rel: Features of distributed OS: resource sharing, scalability, flexibility, reliability. Contrast: network OS (users aware of machines) and tightly coupled multiprocessor (shared memory). Adding nodes to grow capacity = scalability.

qs.stem: _____ computing is a model in which components of a software system are shared among multiple computers.
qs.sol:
Distributed computing is a computing model in which the components of a software system are distributed across multiple computers that work together as a single system.

Answer:  A) Distributed Computing
qs.rel: Distributed computing spreads software components over networked machines. Neighbours: parallel computing (shared memory, tightly coupled), cluster, grid, cloud; client-server and peer-to-peer are architectures.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is a type of Real time operating system?
 I. Hard real time system
 II. Soft real time system
qs.sol:
Real-Time Operating Systems (RTOS) are categorized mainly into two types:

Hard Real-Time System → Strict deadlines must be met; failure can cause system failure (e.g., flight control systems).

Soft Real-Time System → Deadlines are important but not absolutely strict; occasional delays are tolerable (e.g., multimedia systems).

Since both given options (I and II) are valid types of RTOS, the correct answer is Both I and II.
qs.rel: RTOS classes: hard (deadline miss = failure), soft (tolerates misses), firm (late result is useless). Examples: pacemaker/missile hard; video streaming soft. Schedulers: RMS and EDF.

qs.stem: Which one of the following is NOT an Operating System?
qs.sol: The correct answer is LDAP because it stands for Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, which is a network protocol. MS-DOS, iOS, and Linux are all operating systems used to manage computer hardware and software resources.
qs.rel: Protocols and applications are not OSs: LDAP, FTP, HTTP, TCP/IP, Oracle, MS Word. OS examples: UNIX, Linux, DOS, OS/2, Solaris, iOS. System software also includes compilers and loaders which are not OSs.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is a function of an operating system?
 Statements:
 I. Memory allocation
 II. Resource utilization
qs.sol:
An Operating System (OS) acts as a resource manager and a virtual machine provider. Both statements provided are fundamental pillars of OS functionality:

I. Memory Allocation

The OS manages the computer's Primary Memory (RAM). It keeps a record of which parts of memory are currently in use and by whom. Key tasks include:

Allocating memory blocks to processes when they start.

Tracking "free" space to prevent overlaps.

De-allocating memory when a process terminates to prevent memory leaks.

II. Resource Utilization

The OS manages hardware resources like the CPU, Disk, and I/O devices. …
qs.rel: OS functions: process, memory, file, I/O management, protection, accounting, resource allocation. OS acts as resource manager and extended machine. Not OS functions: compiling programs, word processing.

qs.stem: When a program is terminated abnormally, it is called ______.
qs.sol:
Concept

Program termination is the transition in which a running program ceases execution. A normal termination follows the intended completion path, while an abnormal termination ends execution prematurely because of an error, failed assertion, signal, or another exceptional condition.

Application

The blank asks for the technical name of abnormal program termination. In standard programming terminology, to abort a program means to end it abnormally before its normal completion path finishes.

Contrast

End is a broad everyday word for reaching a conclusion; by itself, it does not specify why execution finished. …
qs.rel: Abnormal termination = abort (error, trap, killed). Normal = exit. Related: zombie (finished, not reaped), orphan (parent dead, adopted by init), cascading termination when a parent exits.

qs.stem: Which of the following systems consists of multiple software components that are on multiple computers, but run as a single system?
qs.sol: A distributed computer system runs software components on multiple computers while presenting them as one system.
qs.rel: Distributed system = components on many computers appearing as one. Properties: transparency (location, migration, replication), fault tolerance. Contrast network OS where users see separate machines.

qs.sol: A correct critical-section solution enforces mutual exclusion, permits progress when no process is inside, and bounds how long a waiting process can be overtaken. These are the standard three requirements.
qs.rel: Critical-section solution needs mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. Neighbours: Peterson (2 processes), Bakery (n processes), TestAndSet; these mechanisms do not assume CPU speeds.

qs.sol:
Concept: Bounded waiting means that once a process requests a critical section, there is a finite bound on how many other entries can occur before its own. A synchronization primitive can enforce this only when its waiting policy prevents indefinite overtaking; the primitive name alone is not a fairness guarantee.

Application: A semaphore offers atomic wait and signal operations that can coordinate admission to a shared critical section.

A process executes wait before entering; when access is unavailable, it joins the semaphore waiting queue.

The process leaving the critical section executes signal, making admission available to a waiter. …
qs.rel: Bounded waiting limits how many times others may enter CS after a process requests entry, preventing starvation. Contrast progress (no unnecessary blocking) and mutual exclusion. Deadlock freedom is separate.

qs.sol: Contiguous allocation needs a consecutive extent and works well when file size is fixed or predictable. General-purpose files can grow dynamically, so finding or extending one contiguous extent creates fragmentation and relocation costs.
qs.rel: Contiguous allocation: fast sequential and direct access, external fragmentation, hard to grow files. Contrast linked (slow random access) and indexed (index-block overhead, good direct access).

qs.sol: Replicas hold copies on different nodes, while synchronization propagates updates so the copies converge. That combination preserves a consistent distributed state.
qs.rel: Replication keeps copies on several nodes for availability; synchronization keeps them consistent. Neighbours: fault tolerance, failover, load balancing, consistency vs availability trade-off, RAID mirroring.

qs.sol:
Peterson's algorithm for two processes utilizes three shared variables. These are two flag arrays indicating process intent and a single turn variable to manage access.

Peterson’s Algorithm for synchronization of two processes uses 3 shared variables:

flag[2] → an array of 2 boolean variables to indicate whether a process wants to enter the critical section.

turn → an integer variable to decide whose turn it is.

So, total variables used = 2 flag variables + 1 turn variable = 3 variables.
qs.rel: Peterson's algorithm: two processes, flag[2] and turn; gives mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting. Neighbours: Dekker's algorithm (2 processes), Bakery algorithm (n), not valid on reordering CPUs without barriers.

qs.sol: A process leaves the running state when it must wait for an external event or resource. The blocked queue therefore contains processes awaiting events such as I/O completion, rather than CPU allocation.
qs.rel: Leaving running state: to ready on timeout/preemption, to waiting on I/O or event request, to terminated on exit. Waiting goes only to ready. Ready to running is dispatch.

qs.sol: ReadConsole targets the process console input buffer, such as keystrokes entered in a terminal window. Network, database, and disk-file sources use their respective handles or APIs instead.
qs.rel: ReadConsole reads from the console input buffer (keyboard); ReadFile is general file/device read. Neighbours: WriteConsole, CreateFile, CloseHandle; Windows uses handles; Unix equivalent read(0,...).

qs.stem: Which of the following is not a operating system for mobile computing?
qs.sol:
Concept

An operating system is system software that manages a device’s hardware and provides services for applications. A mobile operating system performs this role on handheld devices such as smartphones and personal digital assistants.

Application

Classify each offered name by what it denotes. Windows Mobile, Palm OS, and Symbian OS denote operating-system platforms used on handheld or smartphone devices. MANET denotes a mobile ad hoc network: a self-configuring wireless-network architecture, not device system software.

Contrast

Windows Mobile: Microsoft’s operating-system platform for handheld devices and smartphones. …
qs.rel: Mobile OS list: Android, iOS, Symbian, Windows Phone, BlackBerry OS, Tizen. Desktop/server OSs such as Windows XP, Ubuntu, Solaris, MS-DOS are the usual distractors.

qs.sol: A contiguous file layout keeps blocks adjacent, giving predictable access time for time-sensitive workloads. With fast direct access and fixed placement, real-time systems are the fitting use case.
qs.rel: Contiguous layout gives predictable access since blocks are adjacent, minimising seeks, and supports direct access easily. Drawbacks: external fragmentation, file growth, need of defragmentation or compaction.

qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: the unqualified wording also allowed later access failures under restrictive sharing, so the effect independent of sharing mode is asked. CreateFile allocates a handle and associated kernel resources. CloseHandle decrements its reference count and releases them when appropriate. Omitting it can retain those resources until process cleanup.
qs.rel: Same file-allocation family: contiguous, linked, indexed. Neighbours: FAT is linked allocation with table; Unix inode uses direct plus indirect pointers; free-space via bit vector.

qs.stem: In a distributed computing environment, multiple computers can provide the same services. This way, if one machine is not available, others can fill in for the service. What is the advantage of this?
qs.sol:
Redundant service providers let another machine take over after one fails.

That provides resilience and redundancy.
qs.rel: Redundant providers give fault tolerance and high availability (failover). Related distributed-system goals: reliability, load sharing, resource sharing; techniques: replication, clustering, heartbeat monitoring.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are FALSE? 

(i) In distributed computing, you may add multiple machines as required. 
(ii) Because of the distribution across multiple servers, troubleshooting and diagnostics are more challenging in distributed computing.
qs.sol: Statement (i) is true because distributed computing allows capacity to be increased by adding more machines or nodes. Statement (ii) is also true because distribution across multiple servers makes troubleshooting, monitoring and diagnostics more complex. Since the question asks which statements are false, neither (i) nor (ii) is false. Therefore, option D is correct.
qs.rel: Distributed computing allows adding machines for scalability and gives fault tolerance via redundancy, but adds complexity, network latency, security and consistency issues. Evaluate each statement against these trade-offs.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements about the OS/2 operating system is correct?

opts.A: It is a single-tasking operating system.
opts.B: It was implemented to be more layered than MS-DOS.
opts.C: It allows direct user access to hardware.
opts.D: MS-DOS is a descendant of OS/2.

qs.sol:
Concept

Operating-system architecture separates user programs from hardware through protected execution modes and system services. OS/2 was designed as a more advanced successor-era system than MS-DOS, with layered organization and multitasking support.

Application

The statement about being more layered than MS-DOS matches that architectural direction. A single-tasking description conflicts with OS/2 multitasking design; unrestricted direct hardware access conflicts with protected-mode operation; and the historical direction is MS-DOS preceding OS/2, not descending from it.

Cross-check

Layered design explains why OS/2 is presented as more structured than MS-DOS. …
qs.rel: OS/2 was a 32-bit multitasking OS developed by IBM and Microsoft (later IBM). Neighbours: MS-DOS single-user single-task, Windows NT, UNIX multiuser. Know which OS is which generation.

qs.sol: On a single-core processor, only one instruction stream executes at any instant. Threading can improve responsiveness and overlap waiting, but it does not create simultaneous computation on that one core.
qs.rel: On a single core only one instruction stream runs at an instant; multitasking is interleaving (concurrency). True parallelism needs multicore or multiprocessors. Related: time slicing, context switch overhead.

qs.stem: Match the following.

opts.A: i – D, ii – C, iii – B, iv – A
opts.B: i – A, ii – B, iii – C, iv – D
opts.C: i – D, ii – A, iii – B, iv – C
opts.D: i – B, ii – C, iii – D, iv – A

qs.sol:
The objective is to match the different types of Operating Systems (OS) with their primary characteristics or performance goals.

Correct Matches:

Batch Processing System — D (CPU idle time): In early batch systems, the CPU often sat idle while waiting for slow I/O devices (like card readers) to load the next job in the batch.

Multiprogramming — C (Resource utilization): The main goal of multiprogramming is to keep the CPU and other resources busy at all times by having multiple jobs ready in memory.

Time sharing — B (Good response time): Time-sharing systems are designed to provide interactive use for multiple users, making quick response time a critical performance metric. …
qs.note: Table/figure from the original paper was not captured. Use the explanation to see the correct matching.
qs.rel: Matching OS types: batch (no interaction, resident monitor), multiprogramming (CPU utilisation), time-sharing (response time), real-time (deadline), distributed (loosely coupled), multiprocessor (tightly coupled, throughput).

topics.deep:
- **OS** = resource manager + extended machine (virtual machine) between user and hardware; also a **control program** (controls execution of user programs and I/O devices). **Functions:** process management, memory management, file management, device/I-O management, protection and security, accounting, command interpretation (user interface), error detection.
- **Goals:** convenience (user view), efficiency (system view). **Kernel** = always-resident core; **shell** = command interpreter; **bootstrap loader** loads kernel at power-on (stored in ROM/firmware).
- **Types of OS:**
| Type | Key idea | Example / trait |
|---|---|---|
| **Batch** | Similar jobs grouped, no user interaction; **resident monitor** sequences jobs; CPU idles during I/O | Early IBM; payroll |
| **Multiprogramming** | Several jobs in memory; CPU switches when one does I/O; goal = **maximise CPU utilisation** | Degree of multiprogramming |
| **Time-sharing (multitasking)** | CPU time sliced (quantum) among users; goal = **minimise response time** | Unix, Linux |
| **Multiprocessor (parallel/tightly coupled)** | Many CPUs sharing memory and clock; higher throughput, graceful degradation | SMP, AMP |
| **Distributed (loosely coupled)** | Independent machines with own memory/clock connected by network, appear as one system | Resource sharing, load sharing, **scalability, flexibility, reliability**, speed |
| **Network OS** | Users aware of multiple machines; file sharing over network | Novell NetWare, Windows Server |
| **Real-time (RTOS)** | Fixed deadlines. **Hard RT** = missing deadline is failure (missile, pacemaker). **Soft RT** = occasional miss tolerated (multimedia). **Firm RT** = result useless after deadline | VxWorks, QNX |
| **Embedded / mobile** | Resource-constrained, dedicated | Android, iOS, Symbian, Windows Phone, BlackBerry OS |
- **Asymmetric multiprocessing:** one master CPU schedules, others slaves. **Symmetric (SMP):** every CPU runs OS tasks; Linux/Windows use SMP.
- **Distributed systems:** advantages = resource sharing, computation speedup, **reliability via redundancy/replication** (if one node fails, another provides the same service), communication. **Replication** = copies of data on different nodes; **synchronization** keeps copies consistent. Fault tolerance, transparency (location, migration, replication, concurrency) are standard terms.
- **Cluster:** group of computers working as one; **grid:** geographically spread; **cloud:** on-demand service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS).
- **Not an OS (common distractors):** **LDAP** (protocol), **FTP, HTTP, TCP/IP** (protocols), **MS Word, Chrome, Oracle** (applications), **BIOS** (firmware), **compiler/assembler** (system software but not OS). **OS examples:** MS-DOS, UNIX, Linux, Windows, macOS, iOS, Android, OS/2 (IBM/Microsoft, successor of DOS era, multitasking, 32-bit), Solaris, Symbian.
- **Not mobile OS:** Windows XP, Ubuntu desktop, MS-DOS, Solaris. Mobile: Android, iOS, Symbian, Windows Phone, Tizen, BlackBerry OS.
- **Program vs process:** program = passive entity on disk; process = active entity (program in execution). **Termination:** normal (exit) vs **abnormal** (abort/crash due to error, trap, killed by parent/OS); abnormal termination is called **aborted/abort**.
- **Critical-section requirements:** **mutual exclusion**, **progress**, **bounded waiting** (no assumption about relative speeds). **Peterson's algorithm:** two processes, **two shared variables** - `flag[2]` and `turn` (flag is an array, so some books count it as "three" values: flag[0], flag[1], turn); satisfies all three requirements; software-only, not for n processes.
- **Disk-space allocation:** **contiguous** (fast sequential and direct access, suffers external fragmentation, file growth hard), **linked** (no external fragmentation, slow direct access, pointer overhead, reliability issue), **indexed** (index block; supports direct access; overhead of index block). Contiguous has **predictable access** because blocks are adjacent (fewer seeks).
- **Windows API:** `ReadConsole` reads from console input buffer; `ReadFile` general; `CreateFile`, `WriteFile`, `CloseHandle`. Handles are used for objects.
- **Single-core CPU:** only one instruction stream executes at an instant - concurrency is by interleaving, not true parallelism; parallelism needs multiple cores.
- **Worked contrast:** Hard RT guarantees deadline; time sharing guarantees only reasonable response; batch gives highest throughput but no interactivity.
- **Typical traps:** "distributed OS" vs "network OS" (transparency); multiprogramming (utilisation) vs multitasking (response time); multiprocessing (many CPUs) vs multiprogramming (many jobs, one CPU); "loosely coupled" = distributed, "tightly coupled" = parallel.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) which is NOT a type of OS; (2) match OS type with goal (throughput, response time, utilisation); (3) hard vs soft real-time examples; (4) tightly vs loosely coupled systems; (5) advantages of distributed systems (scalability, flexibility, reliability, resource sharing) and which is NOT; (6) examples of mobile/embedded OS; (7) asymmetric vs symmetric multiprocessing; (8) three critical-section requirements and Peterson's variables; (9) pros/cons of contiguous vs linked vs indexed allocation; (10) function of resident monitor / bootstrap.

topics.title: 2. System Calls, Kernel Structure & Interfaces
topics.theory:
- **System call** = interface between a running program and the OS (switch to kernel mode). **Categories:** Process control (create, terminate, **wait for time**), File manipulation, Device manipulation/management (request/release device), Information maintenance, **Communication** (create/delete connection, send/receive messages). "Data compilation" is not a category.
- **Parameter passing methods:** in **registers**, in a block/table in memory (address in register), or on the **stack**. Linux uses registers (block when more than registers).
- **Kernel:** innermost layer, **always resident in main memory**. **Monolithic** (Linux, Unix — large kernel, fast) vs **Microkernel** (only essential services in kernel; Mach, MINIX; smaller kernel, easier to extend, message passing) vs **Hybrid** (Windows NT, macOS). **Privileged instructions run only in kernel (supervisor) mode**; user mode vs kernel mode switch via trap/system call.
- **System programs** (editors, compilers, debuggers) help programmers; not part of the core OS.
- **Interfaces:** **CLI** (command line interpreter/shell — text commands), **GUI**, menu-driven, form-based.

qs.stem: Inner most layer of operating system which is always present in main memory is known as ______.
qs.sol: The kernel is the core component of an operating system that resides permanently in main memory. It manages hardware resources and provides essential services for other software layers, making it the innermost layer.
qs.rel: Kernel is the innermost, always-resident layer. Neighbours: shell (outermost interface), system programs, device drivers, bootstrap loader (loads kernel from firmware/disk).

qs.stem: The instruction which is executed only in kernel mode is known as ______.
qs.sol: Privileged instructions are specific commands that can only be executed when the processor is in kernel or supervisor mode. These instructions manage critical system resources and hardware operations, preventing user-mode applications from accessing them directly to ensure system stability and security.
qs.rel: Privileged instructions run only in kernel mode: I/O, set timer, disable interrupts, modify mode bit, clear memory. User-mode attempt raises a trap. Related: dual-mode operation and mode bit.

qs.stem:
Which of the following are monolithic kernel systems?
 I. Linux
 II. Windows
qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: the marked key includes Windows, but Windows uses a hybrid kernel; Linux alone has a monolithic kernel.
qs.rel: Monolithic kernels: UNIX, Linux (with modules), MS-DOS-style. Microkernel: Mach, QNX, Minix. Windows NT is hybrid. Monolithic is fast but less modular; microkernel is more reliable but slower.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are true about microkernel? 
(i) This method reduces the size of the kernel. 
(ii) This approach was used to develop the Mach operating system at Carnegie Mellon University.
qs.sol: A microkernel keeps only essential services in kernel mode and moves other services, such as file systems or device drivers, to user space. This reduces the size of the kernel, so statement (i) is true. The Mach operating system was developed at Carnegie Mellon University and is a classic example associated with the microkernel approach, so statement (ii) is also true.
qs.rel: Microkernel: minimal kernel, services in user space via message passing; easier to extend and port, more reliable and secure, slower due to IPC. Contrast layered (hierarchy) and modular (loadable modules).

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a system call category?
qs.sol:
The correct answer is Option 4: Data Compilation.

System calls provide an interface between a running program and the operating system. They are generally grouped into five or six major categories based on the services they provide. While the OS handles the management of processes, hardware, and data storage, it does not have a "Data Compilation" category, as compilation is typically handled by user-level software like compilers (e.g., GCC or Clang).
qs.rel: System-call categories: process control, file management, device management, information maintenance, communication, protection. Fake categories like data compilation are distractors.

qs.stem: Which of the following system call include ‘wait for time’ operation command in Operating System?
qs.sol: System calls can be grouped by the kind of operating-system action they request. A 'wait for time' operation pauses a running process for a specified interval instead of letting it continue executing immediately. The process normally enters a waiting state until the interval expires, after which it becomes eligible to run again; it need not resume immediately. This concerns the process's execution and state, so it belongs to Process Control, option A. Device Management concerns devices, File Management concerns files, and Communications concerns exchanging data, rather than this timed suspension.
qs.rel: Wait for time/sleep falls under process control. Neighbours: fork, exec, exit, wait, abort, kill; file calls open/read/write/close; communication calls pipe, send, receive.

qs.stem: Which of the following methods is used to pass the parameters in system calls of Linux operating system?
qs.sol:
A system call can receive parameters through a memory block or table.

Linux uses this method: the program places the parameters in memory and passes the block address to the operating system.
qs.rel: Linux/Solaris pass parameters via a memory block/table whose address goes in a register. Other methods: registers (limited count) and stack. Block and stack methods allow unlimited parameters.

qs.stem: According to the standard Operating System Concepts classification, which parameter-passing method is identified as being used by Linux and Solaris for system calls?

opts.B: Using a memory block or table

qs.sol:
System calls need a way to hand arguments from user code to the kernel, and operating-system theory identifies three general techniques for doing this:

Pass the parameters directly in CPU registers.

Store the parameters in a block (table) in memory, and pass only the address of that block in a register.

Push the parameters onto the stack, to be popped off by the operating system.

Register-only passing is simple but is limited by the number of registers available, so it cannot scale to calls with many arguments. …
qs.rel: Parameter-passing: registers, memory block/table, stack. Block method is used by Linux and Solaris; register method is fastest but limited by register count. Know which book classification the stem uses.

qs.stem: Which of the following command is used in the communication system call of an operating system?
qs.sol: Operating-system communication system calls include operations such as attaching or detaching remote devices.
qs.rel: Communication system calls: create/delete connection, send_message, receive_message, shared memory attach. Models: message passing (small data, distributed) vs shared memory (fast, needs sync). Pipe is a Unix IPC.

qs.stem: Which of the following refers to services like editors, debuggers that assist the programmers in creating programs and are not actually part of the operating system but are accessible through the operating system?
qs.sol:
Utilities such as editors and debuggers support program development through services accessible from the operating system.

Utilities supply supporting tools such as editors and debuggers.
qs.rel: Programming-language support utilities: compilers, assemblers, editors, debuggers, interpreters. Other system program groups: file manipulation, status information, loaders, communications, background daemons.

topics.deep:
- **System call** = programmatic interface through which a user process requests a kernel service. Executed via a **trap/software interrupt** that switches CPU from **user mode to kernel mode** (mode bit 1 -> 0 in many texts); return switches back. Accessed normally via an **API** (e.g. POSIX, Win32, Java API) which wraps the call; the **run-time library** has a system-call interface that maps API call to a number indexed in a **system-call table**.
- **Categories of system calls:**
| Category | Unix examples | Windows examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Process control** | fork, exec, exit, wait, abort, kill, **sleep/wait for time**, allocate memory | CreateProcess, ExitProcess, WaitForSingleObject, Sleep |
| **File management** | open, read, write, close, create, delete, lseek | CreateFile, ReadFile, WriteFile, CloseHandle |
| **Device management** | ioctl, read, write, request/release device | SetConsoleMode, ReadConsole, WriteConsole |
| **Information maintenance** | getpid, alarm, time, set attributes | GetCurrentProcessId, SetTimer |
| **Communication** | pipe, shmget, mmap, socket, send/receive (message passing), create/delete connection | CreatePipe, CreateFileMapping |
| **Protection** | chmod, umask, chown | SetFileSecurity |
- **"Wait for time"** belongs to **process control**. "Data compilation" or "data processing" is **not** a system call category.
- **Parameter passing methods (3):** (1) in **registers** (fast, limited count); (2) in a **block/table in memory**, address of block passed in a register - **used by Linux and Solaris** (for more than 5 params); (3) pushed on the **stack** by program and popped by OS. Block and stack methods have no limit on number of parameters.
- **Communication models:** **message passing** (send/receive, good for small data and distributed systems, no conflicts) and **shared memory** (shmget/shmat, faster, needs synchronisation). Commands in this area: `send_message`, `receive_message`, `pipe()`, `socket()`.
- **Dual mode operation:** user mode and kernel (supervisor/monitor/privileged) mode, a **mode bit** in hardware. **Privileged instructions** (I/O, set timer, clear memory, disable interrupts, modify mode bit, context switch) execute **only in kernel mode**; attempting in user mode raises a trap.
- **Kernel** = innermost layer, always resident in main memory; interface between hardware and applications. **Shell** = outer interface.
- **Kernel structures:**
| Structure | Idea | Example | Trait |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Monolithic** | All OS services in one big kernel space | **Linux**, traditional UNIX, MS-DOS (no protection) | Fast (little overhead), less reliable and hard to maintain; one bug can crash kernel |
| **Layered** | OS split in layers 0..N, each uses only lower layer | THE OS | Easy debug/verification; overhead, layer ordering hard |
| **Microkernel** | Only essentials (IPC, basic scheduling, memory, address space) in kernel; others (file system, drivers, networking) as **user-space servers** | **Mach**, QNX, Minix | Easier extension, portable, more secure/reliable; **slower** due to message-passing overhead |
| **Modular (loadable kernel modules)** | Core + dynamically loadable modules | **Linux** (modules), Solaris | Flexible like microkernel but direct calls |
| **Hybrid** | Mix of monolithic and microkernel | **Windows NT**, macOS (XNU) | Compromise |
| **Virtual machine / exokernel** | Each user sees a virtual copy of hardware | VMware, JVM | Isolation |
- **Microkernel true statements:** reduces kernel size, easier to extend, easier to port, more reliable/secure (less code in kernel mode), performance overhead from user-kernel communication. **Windows is generally classed hybrid** (some books say monolithic-like; check option wording).
- **System programs (utilities):** file manipulation, status information, **programming-language support (compilers, assemblers, debuggers, interpreters)**, **editors**, program loading and execution, communications, background services (daemons), application programs. "Services like editors, debuggers that assist programmers" = **program development utilities / programming-language support**.
- **OS services:** user interface (CLI, GUI, batch), program execution, I/O operations, file-system manipulation, communication, error detection, resource allocation, accounting, protection and security.
- **Policy vs mechanism:** mechanism = how; policy = what. Microkernels separate them.
- **Boot sequence:** power-on -> BIOS/UEFI POST -> bootloader (GRUB) -> kernel loaded -> init/systemd.
- **Typical traps:** fork is a system call, `printf` is a library function that eventually calls `write`; `exec` replaces image; system call vs library function; user threads vs kernel threads; "API" is not the same as system call.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) classify a call (fork, wait, open, pipe) into its category; (2) how many ways to pass parameters and which does Linux use; (3) which instruction runs only in kernel mode (privileged); (4) monolithic vs microkernel comparisons, examples; (5) mode bit value/dual-mode concept; (6) layered approach advantage/disadvantage; (7) hybrid kernel examples; (8) which is NOT an OS service; (9) trap vs interrupt vs exception; (10) what a system call table or API does.

topics.title: 3. Linux — Shell, Commands & File System
topics.theory:
- **Shell** = command interpreter (bash, sh, csh). **Redirection:** `<` input, `>` output (overwrite), `>>` append, `2>` stderr, `|` pipe. `!` is history expansion, not redirection. Shell script = batch file of commands (`.sh`).
- **Process creation:** **`fork()` creates a new process (copy of parent); `exec()` replaces its image with a new program** (fork first, then exec).
- **Directory layout:** `/` root, **`/etc` = system configuration files**, `/home` user home directories, `/bin` & `/usr/bin` commands, `/dev` device files, `/var` logs/variable data, `/tmp` temporary, `/proc` process info, `/mnt` mount points.
- **Special files** in `ls -l` first column: `-` regular, **`d` directory**, **`c` character special**, `b` block special, `l` symlink, `s` socket, `p` pipe.
- **Commands:** `grep`, `egrep`, `fgrep` search content inside files (`find` locates files by name/attributes); **`touch` and `cat > file` create files**; `ls`, `cd`, `pwd`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `mkdir`, `chmod` (permissions), `chown`, `ps`, `kill`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `sort`.
- **Mounting** (`mount`) makes a file system/directory visible in multiple parts of the file tree (links: hard and symbolic).

qs.stem: The type of interaction between a user and a computer involving commands and responses with one person at a time is called: ______
qs.sol:
A command line interface takes typed commands and returns responses in an interactive dialogue.

A graphical interface is defined by visual controls rather than command-response text.
qs.rel: CLI: typed commands and text responses. Contrast GUI (icons, windows) and batch interface. Shell is the command line interpreter; bash is the default Linux shell.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT an input/output redirection symbol that Linux shell uses?
qs.sol: In the Linux shell (like Bash), the ! symbol is used for history expansion (e.g., !! repeats the last command) or as a logical NOT operator in scripts and expressions. It is not used for standard input/output redirection.
qs.rel: Redirection: > overwrite, >> append, < input, 2> stderr, | pipe. The ! sign is history expansion. File descriptors 0, 1, 2 = stdin, stdout, stderr.

qs.stem: Which of following is a text-based program that the user invokes to interact with the system software?
qs.sol:
A command line interpreter accepts text commands from the user and passes requests to the operating system.

This is the text-based interface described.
qs.rel: Text-based program for user to talk to system software = command line interpreter/shell. Types: bash, sh, csh, ksh, zsh. Shell script is a stored sequence of shell commands.

qs.stem: In a Linux Operating System, a new process is created by the ____ system call, and a new program is run after a call to ____.
qs.sol:
fork() creates a new process by duplicating the caller. exec() replaces the process image with a new program.

Creation precedes program replacement.
qs.rel: New process via fork() (child gets 0, parent gets child PID); new program via exec() which replaces process image. wait() lets parent collect child; zombie and orphan processes follow.

qs.stem: Which of the following in an operating system refers to batch file that commands the command interpreter?
qs.sol:
A shell script file conventionally uses the sh extension or shell name and contains commands for a command interpreter.

It denotes the shell-command batch file here.
qs.rel: Shell script = batch file of commands for the interpreter, extension .sh, starts with #!/bin/bash and needs execute permission (chmod +x). DOS counterpart is .bat.

qs.stem: _____ is a symbol used to represent special files in Linux OS.
qs.sol:
Option 3: c

In Linux, when you use the ls -l command to list files, the first character of the permission string indicates the file type. The symbol 'c' represents Character Special files (also known as character device files), which are used to represent hardware devices that transmit data character-by-character, such as keyboards or serial ports.
qs.rel: ls -l first char: - file, d directory, l symlink, c character special, b block special, p pipe, s socket. Device files live in /dev (c for terminals, b for disks).

qs.stem: What does  /etc  directory contain in Linux operating system?

opts.A: Home directories of the common user
opts.D: Common program shared by the system and the system administrator

qs.sol: In the Linux Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS), the /etc directory is one of the most critical locations on the system. It is reserved for host-specific system-wide configuration files. These files control the behavior of the operating system and various installed applications—for example, network settings, user account information (/etc/passwd), and startup scripts. A key rule for /etc is that it should only contain configuration data and not binary executables.
qs.rel: /etc holds system configuration files (passwd, fstab, hosts). Contrast /var (logs), /dev (devices), /home (users), /bin (commands), /proc (process info), /tmp.

qs.stem:
Which of the following Linux commands is/are used to search content from files?
 commands:
 i) grep
 ii) egrep
 iii) fgrep
 iv) find
 v) tail
 vi) tr
qs.sol:
Option 1: i, ii and iii only

The grep family of commands is specifically designed for searching plain-text data sets for lines that match a regular expression.

grep: The standard Global Regular Expression Print command.

egrep: (Extended grep) used for searching using extended regular expressions.

fgrep: (Fixed grep) used for searching for fixed strings rather than regular expressions, which is faster for simple text searches
qs.rel: Searching file content: grep, egrep (extended regex), fgrep (fixed strings). Searching file names uses find or locate. Options: -i, -v, -n, -r, -c.

qs.stem:
Which of the following commands is/are used to create files in Linux?
 Commands:
 i) touch
 ii) cat
 iii) head
 iv) finger
qs.sol:
In the Linux operating system, files can be created using various commands, but they must have the functional capability to generate a new entry in the file system.

i) touch: This is the most common command used to create an empty file. It is primarily used to update timestamps, but if the file does not exist, it creates it.

ii) cat: While primarily used to display file contents, the cat command can create a file when used with the redirection operator (e.g., cat > filename.txt). This allows a user to input text directly into a new file.

The other commands listed (head and finger) are used for viewing data or system information and do not have a built-in function to create new files.
qs.rel: File creation: touch (empty file), cat > file, echo > file, editors, cp. head/tail just display parts of files. mkdir creates directories.

qs.stem: _____ is a system to make a file or directory visible in multiple parts of the system’s file tree in Linux operating system.
qs.sol:
The correct answer is Option 3: Links.

In the Linux operating system, links are used to create references to a file or directory in different locations within the file system hierarchy. This allows the same file to be accessed from multiple paths without duplicating the actual data on the disk. There are two primary types of links:

Hard Links: These point directly to the inode of the file.

Symbolic (Soft) Links: These act like shortcuts that point to the filename/path of the original file.
qs.rel: Links make a file reachable from several places. Hard link: same inode, same filesystem, survives deletion of the original. Symbolic link: path pointer, can cross filesystems, dangles if target removed.

topics.deep:
- **Linux** = open-source, UNIX-like, multiuser, multitasking OS created by **Linus Torvalds (1991)**; kernel is monolithic with loadable modules. **Shell** = command interpreter; types: **bash (Bourne Again SHell, default)**, sh, csh, ksh, zsh. A **CLI/CUI** (command line interface) = text commands and responses; GUI = windows/icons.
- **A text-based program that lets the user interact with system software** = command line interpreter (shell). **Shell script** = batch file of commands run by the shell, conventionally with `.sh` extension, begins with `#!/bin/bash` (shebang); make executable with `chmod +x`. DOS equivalent is `.bat` file.
- **I/O redirection and pipes:** `>` redirect stdout (overwrite), `>>` append, `<` stdin from file, `2>` stderr, `2>&1` merge stderr to stdout, `|` pipe stdout of one command to stdin of next, `<<` here-document. File descriptors: **0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr**. `!` is **history expansion** (e.g. `!!` last command), not redirection. `&` runs in background, `;` separates commands.
- **Process creation:** `fork()` creates a child (copy of caller; returns 0 to child, child PID to parent, -1 on failure); `exec()` family replaces process image with new program; `wait()` parent waits for child; `exit()` terminate. A shell runs a command via fork + exec. **Zombie** = terminated but not yet reaped by parent; **orphan** = parent died, adopted by init (PID 1). `getpid()`, `getppid()`.
- **Standard directory structure (FHS):**
| Directory | Content |
|---|---|
| `/` | root of tree |
| `/bin`, `/usr/bin` | executable user commands |
| `/sbin` | system admin binaries |
| `/etc` | **system configuration files** (passwd, shadow, fstab, hosts) |
| `/home` | users' home directories |
| `/root` | root user's home |
| `/dev` | **device files** |
| `/proc` | virtual FS of process/kernel info |
| `/var` | variable data: logs (`/var/log`), spool, mail |
| `/tmp` | temporary files |
| `/usr` | user programs, libraries |
| `/lib` | shared libraries |
| `/boot` | kernel, bootloader |
| `/mnt`, `/media` | mount points |
- **File types in `ls -l` first character:** `-` regular, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link, **`c` character special file**, **`b` block special file**, `p` named pipe (FIFO), `s` socket.
- **Permissions:** `rwx` for user/group/others; r=4, w=2, x=1. `chmod 755 f` = rwxr-xr-x; `chmod u+x f`; `chown user:group f`; `umask` sets default mask (default files 666 minus umask, dirs 777 minus umask; umask 022 -> 644 files, 755 dirs).
- **Searching content:** `grep` (basic regex), `egrep`/`grep -E` (extended regex), `fgrep`/`grep -F` (fixed strings). Options: `-i` ignore case, `-v` invert, `-n` line numbers, `-r` recursive, `-c` count. `find` searches files by name/attribute (`find / -name x`), `locate` uses a database, `which` finds executable path. `awk`, `sed` process text.
- **Creating files:** `touch` (empty file or update timestamp), `cat > file` (type content, Ctrl+D ends), `echo text > file`, editors (vi, nano), `cp`. `head`/`tail` only **display** first/last 10 lines - they do not create. `mkdir` creates directory; `rmdir` removes empty dir; `rm -r` recursive.
- **Common commands:** `ls`, `cd`, `pwd`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `cat`, `more`, `less`, `wc` (lines/words/bytes), `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `diff`, `tar`, `ps`, `top`, `kill` (`kill -9` SIGKILL), `df`, `du`, `mount`, `man`, `whoami`, `who`, `date`, `echo`, `chmod`, `passwd`.
- **Links:** make a file visible at multiple places in tree. **Hard link** (`ln src dst`): another name for the same inode, same filesystem only, cannot link directories, survives deletion of the original, link count increases. **Symbolic/soft link** (`ln -s src dst`): separate file holding path, can cross filesystems and point to directories, **dangling** if target deleted. `ls -l` shows `l` and `->`.
- **Inode:** structure holding metadata (owner, permissions, size, timestamps, block pointers) but **not the filename** (name lives in directory entry).
- **Absolute vs relative path:** absolute begins at `/`; relative begins from current directory (`.` current, `..` parent, `~` home).
- **Typical traps:** `>` overwrites while `>>` appends; hard link vs soft link behaviour on deletion; `/etc` config vs `/dev` devices vs `/var` logs; `c` vs `b` vs `d` type letters; `grep` for content vs `find` for filenames.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) meaning of chmod 644/755/777; (2) difference hard vs soft link; (3) which directory holds logs / devices / home; (4) what fd 2 is; (5) result of `ls -l` first character `b`/`p`/`l`; (6) which command shows last lines or counts words; (7) what `fork` returns to the child; (8) zombie vs orphan; (9) purpose of `|` in `cmd1 | cmd2`; (10) default shell in Linux.

topics.title: 4. Processes, Threads & CPU Scheduling
topics.theory:
- **Process states:** New → Ready → Running → Waiting (Blocked) → Terminated (no "Excite" state). Running → Ready on preemption/timeslice; Running → Waiting on I/O request; **Blocked → Ready** when I/O completes. A process in memory = text, data, **heap, stack**.
- **PCB (Process Control Block)** stores process state, program counter, CPU registers, scheduling info, memory info, I/O status (not network interface config). **Thread** = lightweight process (shares code/data/files, own stack/registers/PC); process = unit of protection/resource ownership, thread = unit of concurrency.
- **Schedulers:** **Long-term (job) scheduler** controls the degree of multiprogramming; **short-term (CPU) scheduler** is the fastest, runs most often; medium-term does swapping. **Dispatcher** gives CPU control to the selected process (context switch, switch to user mode, jump to program). Queues: job queue, **ready queue**, device queue.
- **Criteria:** CPU utilisation, **throughput = processes completed per unit time**, turnaround time (completion − arrival), waiting time (turnaround − burst), response time.
- **Algorithms:** FCFS (non-preemptive, convoy effect), **SJF/SJN** (optimal average waiting time; starvation), **SRTF** (preemptive SJF), Round Robin (time quantum; preemptive), Priority (starvation → aging), multilevel queue/feedback. **C-SCAN/SCAN are disk scheduling**, not CPU scheduling.
- **Multiprocessing** = more than one CPU; multiprogramming = many programs in memory; multitasking = time-sharing of CPU.

qs.stem: Which of the following is not a state of a process in operating system?
qs.sol:
English:

In an Operating System, a process can be in the following standard states:

New

Ready

Running

Waiting (Blocked)

Terminated

Among the given options:

Waiting, Running, Ready are valid process states.

Excite is not a valid process state in OS.

👉 Therefore, the correct answer is B (Excite).
qs.rel: Process states: new, ready, running, waiting/blocked, terminated (plus suspended states). Words like sleeping/hold are not standard. Transitions: admit, dispatch, timeout, I/O wait, I/O completion, exit.

qs.stem: A ______ is the subset of a process and is also known as the lightweight process.
qs.sol: A thread is a subset of a process and is also known as the lightweight process. Threads share memory and resources with their parent process, allowing for efficient concurrent execution within a single application.
qs.rel: Thread = lightweight process sharing code, data, heap, files; own stack, PC, registers. Neighbours: user vs kernel threads, many-to-one/one-to-one/many-to-many models, thread pool.

qs.stem: What is the full form of the PCB that is used to store information of a process?
qs.sol: PCB stands for Process Control Block. It is a data structure in the operating system kernel containing information about a specific process.
qs.rel: PCB (Process Control Block) holds state, PC, registers, scheduling and memory info, accounting, I/O status. Neighbours: TCB for threads, ready queue of PCBs, context switch saves to PCB.

qs.stem: Which of the following is not a CPU scheduling Algorithm?
qs.sol:
Concept

An operating system uses different families of scheduling algorithms for different resources. A CPU scheduling algorithm decides the order in which ready processes are given the processor (minimising waiting/turnaround time), whereas a disk scheduling algorithm decides the order in which pending read/write requests are served by the disk arm (minimising seek time). The two solve unrelated problems, so an algorithm belongs to exactly one family.

Applying it here

Classify each listed algorithm by the resource it manages:

FCFS (First Come First Served) — orders processes for the CPU by arrival time. CPU scheduling. …
qs.rel: Scheduling algorithms: FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Priority, RR, multilevel queue, MLFQ. Not CPU scheduling: SCAN, SSTF (disk), LRU (page replacement), Banker's (deadlock).

qs.stem: Which of the following schedulers is the fastest?
qs.sol:
The short-term scheduler chooses the next ready process whenever the CPU needs work.

It runs most frequently and must make decisions very quickly.
qs.rel: Short-term scheduler is fastest (every few ms); long-term slowest; medium-term swaps. Short-term = CPU scheduler, long-term = job scheduler, medium-term = swapper.

qs.stem: Information about each process in an operating system is maintained by ____.
qs.sol:
Option 2: Process Control Block (PCB)

The Process Control Block (PCB) is a data structure used by the operating system to store all the information necessary to manage a particular process. It acts as a "passport" for the process, containing details like the process ID, state, priority, program counter, and CPU registers.
qs.rel: PCB keeps per-process information. Neighbours: process table, thread control block, file descriptor table, page table (referenced from PCB).

qs.stem: What is Throughput in process scheduling?

opts.A: Time required to complete a process
opts.B: Number of processes completed per unit time
opts.C: Time required by a process to respond
opts.D: Time required to abort a process

qs.sol:
Option 2: Number of processes completed per unit time

In Operating Systems, Throughput is a performance metric used to measure the efficiency of a scheduling algorithm. It represents the amount of work the CPU is getting done by counting how many processes finish their execution within a specific timeframe (e.g., 10 processes per second). Higher throughput generally indicates a more efficient scheduler.
qs.rel: Throughput = processes completed per unit time. Other criteria: CPU utilisation, turnaround time, waiting time, response time. Maximise first two, minimise the others.

qs.stem: Which of the following information is NOT included in Process Control Block (PCB)?
qs.sol:
The PCB stores process state, CPU registers and scheduling data.

Network interface configuration is not a standard per-process PCB field.
qs.rel: PCB holds process state, registers, PC, scheduling data, memory limits, open-file list. It does not hold network protocol data or other applications' data.

qs.stem: A process is a(n) ________ entity, whereas a program is a(n) ________ entity.
qs.sol: A process is an active entity representing a program in execution with allocated resources and state. In contrast, a program is a passive entity consisting of static code stored on disk until it is loaded into memory.
qs.rel: Process is active entity, program is passive. Neighbours: process image layout (text, data, heap, stack), one program can create many processes, program counter belongs to process.

qs.stem: Suppose that a process is in 'BLOCKED' state waiting for some I/O service. When the service is completed, it goes to the ____ state.
qs.sol: When a process in the BLOCKED state finishes waiting for I/O, it transitions to the READY state. This occurs because the process is now prepared to execute but requires CPU scheduling before moving to RUNNING.
qs.rel: I/O completion: waiting/blocked -> ready (not directly running). Other transitions: ready->running by dispatcher, running->ready by timeout, running->waiting on I/O request.

qs.stem: Which scheduler controls the degree of multiprogramming i.e., the number of processes in memory?
qs.sol:
The long-term scheduler admits jobs into memory, setting the degree of multiprogramming.

It controls admission of processes to memory.
qs.rel: Long-term scheduler controls degree of multiprogramming and process mix. Short-term picks CPU process; medium-term swaps to reduce degree. Time-sharing OSs often lack a long-term scheduler.

qs.stem: Which of the following modules is involved in CPU scheduling that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler?
qs.sol: The dispatcher transfers CPU control to the process chosen by the short-term scheduler.
qs.rel: Dispatcher does context switch, switch to user mode, jumps to program location. Dispatch latency is its delay. Scheduler selects, dispatcher assigns.

qs.stem: Move the read/write head of disk in or out to position on a correct track is known as ______.
qs.sol: The movement of the read/write head to position it on a specific track is called seeking. The time taken for this operation is known as Seek time.
qs.rel: Seek time = moving head to the right track; rotational latency = waiting for sector; transfer time = reading data. Access time = sum of these.

qs.stem: Which of the following queues keeps a set of all processes residing in main memory ready and waiting to execute?
qs.sol:
The ready queue holds processes in main memory that are ready for CPU execution.

The CPU scheduler selects a process from this queue.
qs.rel: Ready queue holds processes in memory ready to run; device/I/O queues hold waiting ones. Job queue contains all processes in system. Queue elements are PCBs.

qs.stem: Which of the following type of operating systems does not need CPU scheduling?
qs.sol: CPU scheduling is the mechanism an operating system uses to decide which process gets access to the CPU and for how long. This becomes essential when multiple processes are running concurrently, as seen in multi-tasking or time-sharing systems. In these environments, the OS must efficiently switch between tasks to ensure responsiveness and fairness.\nHowever, Single-User Single-Tasking operating systems are designed to run only one program at a time for a single user. Since there is no competition for the CPU among multiple processes, the system does not need to make scheduling decisions. …
qs.rel: Single-process, single-user systems (e.g. MS-DOS) need no CPU scheduling. Multiprogramming, time sharing, multiprocessor and real-time systems all do.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a section of process layout when a process is loaded into the main memory?
qs.sol:
A typical process address space contains text, heap, and stack sections.

A graph is a data structure, not a standard process layout section.
qs.rel: Process image sections: text (code), data, heap (grows up), stack (grows down). Registers and file tables belong to PCB, not to the memory layout.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are true regarding processes and threads in operating system?
 I. Threads encapsulate concurrency within a process.
 II. Process encapsulates protection within the system.
qs.sol:
The correct answer is Option 3: Both I and II.

In modern operating systems, the concepts of processes and threads serve two distinct but complementary purposes:

Statement I: A thread is the basic unit of CPU utilization and represents a single flow of control. By having multiple threads within a single process, the system can perform multiple tasks concurrently (like a web browser downloading an image while simultaneously rendering text). Thus, threads encapsulate concurrency.

Statement II: A process provides an execution environment with its own private address space. …
qs.rel: Threads in a process share code, data, files, heap; have separate stack, registers and PC. Process is the unit of protection and resource ownership; thread is unit of CPU scheduling.

qs.stem: Which of the following part of operating system allocates the CPU to next scheduled process in the system?
qs.sol:
Concept

CPU scheduling separates selection from dispatch. A scheduler chooses the next ready process according to a scheduling policy, while a dispatcher performs the context switch and transfers processor control to the selected process.

Application

The stem asks for the component that hands CPU control to a process after the scheduler has selected it. That operational handoff is performed by the dispatcher.

Contrast

A file manager organizes files, directories, storage access, and permissions.

A scheduler selects the next ready process according to a scheduling policy.

An input/output handler coordinates device requests, interrupts, and data transfer. …
qs.rel: Dispatcher allocates the CPU to the process chosen by the short-term scheduler. Scheduler selects; dispatcher hands over (context switch). Do not confuse with swapper or loader.

qs.stem: Which of the following processor schedulers selects a job currently loaded in the memory and allocates a processor to it?
qs.sol:
The short-term scheduler chooses a ready process already in memory for the CPU.

Medium-term scheduling instead controls suspension and resumption.
qs.rel: Short-term scheduler selects from in-memory ready processes and allocates CPU. Long-term picks from job pool on disk; medium-term swaps. Short-term runs most frequently.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are true regarding threads in operating system?
 I. The threads in a process are visible to other processes.
 II. A thread is strictly private resource of a process.
qs.sol:
CONCEPT

A process is an operating system protection and resource-ownership boundary. Threads are execution paths inside that boundary: they share process resources, while each thread keeps its own stack, registers, and execution state.

Peer processes communicate through explicit inter-process communication (IPC); they do not ordinarily use another process’s internal threads directly. The operating system kernel and authorized diagnostic tools may still inspect threads, which is different from visibility to an ordinary peer process. …
qs.rel: Threads of one process share address space and resources, so inter-thread communication is cheap; creation and context switch faster than for processes. One thread's stack is private.

qs.stem: Which of the following type of operating systems refers to the idea of keeping the processor as busy as possible, by executing multiple programs simultaneously, that are loaded into memory, and the processor switches rapidly among them?
qs.sol:
Multiprogramming keeps several programs in memory and switches the processor among them to reduce idle time.

Multiprogramming overlaps the residence of programs and switches CPU service among them.
qs.rel: Multiprogramming keeps CPU busy by switching when a job waits. Time sharing aims at response time; batch at throughput; real-time at deadlines. Degree of multiprogramming = processes in memory.

qs.stem: Which of the following statement(s) is/are NOT correct? I. Parallel processing is also known as loosely coupled architecture. II. Distributed system is also known as tightly coupled architecture.
qs.sol: In this standard architectural distinction, parallel processors share closely coordinated resources and are tightly coupled. Distributed computers communicate over a network and are loosely coupled. Statement I swaps the coupling of parallel systems, and statement II swaps that of distributed systems; both are incorrect.
qs.rel: Parallel processing = tightly coupled (shared memory, common clock); distributed = loosely coupled (own memory, network). Check statements against this reversal trap.

qs.stem: Which of the following processes generates I/O requests infrequently, using most of its time doing computations?
qs.sol: The English stem says I/O requests are infrequent, which describes a CPU-bound process. The printed Hindi says “बार-बार” (frequently), which would instead describe an I/O-bound process; this is a contradiction in the paper, and the official key follows the English wording.
qs.rel: CPU-bound process: long computation, rare I/O requests. I/O-bound: many short CPU bursts. A good long-term scheduler mixes both. Burst pattern starts and ends with CPU burst.

qs.stem: Which of the following type of operating systems allows multiple users to simultaneously access the system through terminals, with the operating systems interleaving the execution of each user program in a short burst or quantum of computation?
qs.sol:
Time sharing divides processor time into short quanta so several terminal users can interact with the system.

Time sharing interleaves users’ programs in short CPU quanta.
qs.rel: Time-sharing: CPU time sliced among many interactive users giving each fast response; uses round-robin with quantum. Contrast multiprogramming (utilisation) and batch (no interaction).

qs.stem: Data structure maintained by the operating system to maintain information for each thread within a process is known as ______.
qs.sol: The data structure maintained by the operating system to store information about each thread within a process is known as the Thread Control Block (TCB). It contains thread-specific data such as the thread ID, program counter, register set, stack pointer, and thread state. This structure allows the OS to manage and switch between threads efficiently.
qs.rel: Per-thread data lives in the thread control block (TCB): thread id, registers, PC, stack pointer, state. PCB is per process; threads share PCB-level resources.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are true about process states? 
(i) A running process moves to ready state when it is interrupted. 
(ii) A process moves to waiting state when it has completed its execution.
qs.sol:
Concept: A process in the ready state can run but is waiting for CPU time. A running process is using the CPU; preemption can return unfinished work to ready. Waiting means unfinished work is blocked on an event, whereas terminated means execution has ended.

Application:

For statement (i), consider a timer interrupt that preempts a running process before it finishes. The operating system saves its context; because it can run again, it returns to the ready queue.

For statement (ii), consider a process that executes its final instruction and exits. Its work is complete, so it enters the terminated state rather than waiting for an event. …
qs.rel: State rules: running -> ready (preemption/timeout), running -> waiting (I/O), waiting -> ready (event), ready -> running (dispatch). A ready process cannot jump to waiting.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are correct for context switching in Operating System?
I. When a context switch occurs, the kernel saves the context of the old process in its PCB (Process Control Block).
II. Context-Switch time is pure overhead, because the system does no useful work while switching.
qs.sol: During a context switch, the kernel saves the old process context in its PCB. The switch consumes CPU time without doing user-process work, so context-switch time is overhead.
qs.rel: Context switch: save old process's state to its PCB, load new one's; pure overhead, no useful work, time depends on hardware (registers, MMU). Switching threads of one process is cheaper.

qs.stem: Match the following Process states of Operating System with their definitions.
qs.sol: New means the process is being created, Running means instructions are being executed, and Ready means the process is waiting to be assigned to a processor. Therefore the matching is I-3, II-2, III-1.

head: State
Definition
rows: The process is waiting to be assigned to a processor

qs.rel: New = being created, Ready = waiting for CPU, Running = executing, Waiting = waiting for event/I/O, Terminated = finished. Process creation uses fork; PCB moves between queues.

qs.stem: In ________, one thread immediately terminates the target thread.
qs.sol:
Concept

Thread cancellation is a request to end a target thread before its normal completion. Cancellation state controls whether a request can take effect, while cancellation type controls when an enabled request can take effect.

Asynchronous delivery can interrupt execution at an arbitrary point. Deferred delivery postpones cancellation until a defined cancellation point, allowing safer coordination with resource use.

Application

Suppose a target thread is performing a calculation and another thread sends a cancellation request. Assume cancellation is enabled and the calculation has not reached a cancellation point. …
qs.rel: Asynchronous cancellation: one thread terminates target at once; deferred: target checks cancellation points. Related: thread pool, signal handling, thread-specific data.

qs.stem: Which of the following operating systems used non-preemptive scheduling for application multitasking?
qs.sol:
Concept

Preemptive scheduling allows the operating-system kernel to interrupt a running task and give the processor to another runnable task. The task does not have to surrender the processor voluntarily.

In non-preemptive, or cooperative, multitasking, a running application keeps control until it yields, blocks, or finishes. Therefore, one application that does not yield can delay other applications.

Application

Windows 3.1 used cooperative multitasking among Windows applications. Each application processed messages and was expected to return control so that another application could run.

Contrast

Unix uses kernel-managed preemptive time-sharing among runnable processes. …
qs.rel: Non-preemptive multitasking: Windows 3.x and classic Mac OS (cooperative). Preemptive: Windows 95/NT onwards, Linux, UNIX. Preemption needs timer interrupt.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a device management task in an operating system?

opts.A: Installing device and component-level drivers and related software.
opts.C: Implementing device security measures and processes.

qs.sol:
Device management covers drivers, configuration and device security.

Primary memory management is a separate operating-system function.
qs.rel: Device management: drivers, configuration, buffering, spooling, device security. CPU scheduling is processor management, not device management.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements is correct about dynamic loading of the process?

opts.A: In this case, the size of the process cannot exceed the size of the physical memory.
opts.B: In this case, a routine is loaded in the memory when it is called.
opts.C: In this case, an unused routine may be loaded in the memory.
opts.D: It results in worst memory utilisation.

qs.sol: Dynamic loading means a routine is loaded into memory only when it is called. Routines that are never called remain on disk, so memory is not wasted on unused code. Therefore, the correct statement is that a routine is loaded in memory when it is called.
qs.rel: Dynamic loading loads a routine only when called, saving memory; needs no OS support. Dynamic linking postpones linking until run time (shared libraries/DLLs).

qs.stem: During CPU scheduling, processes alternate between two states where process execution begins with ____ and is followed by ____.

opts.A: an I/O burst, a memory burst
opts.B: a memory burst, an I/O burst
opts.C: an I/O burst, a CPU burst
opts.D: a CPU burst, an I/O burst

qs.sol:
A process normally begins with a CPU burst, then performs an I/O burst; the two alternate over its lifetime.

This is the standard CPU-then-I/O burst sequence.
qs.rel: Process execution alternates CPU burst and I/O burst; starts and ends with CPU burst. Burst-length histogram is exponential with many short CPU bursts.

qs.stem: When a process switches from the running state to the waiting state or when a process terminates, the resulting scheduling scheme is called ____.
qs.sol:
These transitions force the current process to relinquish the CPU; the scheme described is non-preemptive.

The printed answer says 'nonprimitive', which is a paper typo retained in the option.
qs.rel: Decision points 1 (running->waiting) and 4 (terminate) give non-preemptive scheduling. Points 2 (running->ready) and 3 (waiting->ready) permit preemption.

qs.stem: Which of the following determines how the process manager can determine that it is time to multiplex the cup and how a thread can be allocated to and removed from the CPU?
qs.sol:
A scheduling mechanism specifies how the manager multiplexes the CPU and assigns or removes threads.

A policy instead decides which eligible thread should run.
qs.rel: The scheduling mechanism determines when the process manager multiplexes the CPU, typically on clock interrupt/time slice expiry. Timer and interrupts enable time sharing.

qs.stem: Which of the following situations does not affect the CPU scheduling decision?

opts.A: When a process switches from the running state to the waiting state.
opts.B: When a process switches from the running state to the ready state.
opts.D: When a process is in execution state.

qs.sol:
Concept

A CPU scheduling decision is reconsidered when the running process undergoes a state transition that releases the CPU or changes queue membership. Remaining in the running state is not a transition.

Application

Running → waiting: a block such as I/O wait releases the CPU, so another scheduling decision can occur.

Running → ready: preemption moves the process to the ready queue, requiring a scheduling choice.

Termination: the process leaves the system and its CPU allocation becomes available for a new choice.

Execution state: the process is still using the CPU; no state transition has occurred at that instant. …
qs.rel: Scheduling is reconsidered at: running->waiting, running->ready, waiting->ready, termination. Events not changing process state (e.g. a new process in new state only) do not trigger it.

qs.stem:
Which of the following statements is/are true about preemptive type process scheduling in an operating system? 
(i) In preemptive scheduling, the utilisation of CPU is low.
(ii) Shortest Job First process scheduling is an example of preemptive scheduling.
qs.sol: Statement (i) is false because preemptive scheduling typically improves CPU utilization by allowing context switches to prioritize shorter jobs. Statement (ii) is false since Shortest Job First (SJF) is non-preemptive by default; its preemptive variant is Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF). Thus, neither statement is correct.
qs.rel: Preemptive scheduling needs timer, shared-data care and can cause more context switches; improves response time but may starve long jobs (SRTF). Non-preemptive: FCFS, non-pre SJF.

qs.stem: Which of the following buffering techniques involves the saving of information in the memory and then writing it to the device while the process continues execution?
qs.sol:
Output buffering holds output data in memory before the device writes it while the process continues.

It decouples the process from the slower output device.
qs.rel: Output buffering stores data in memory then writes in bulk to the device; input buffering reads ahead. Spooling uses disk, buffering uses memory. Double buffering overlaps I/O.

qs.stem: Assuming preemptive priority scheduling, which event neither blocks the running process nor preempts it to the ready state?

opts.A: If a process requests an Input/Output operation
opts.B: If a higher priority process arrived
opts.C: If a lower priority process arrived
opts.D: If a process waits for some action performed by another process

qs.sol:
Modified from the official paper: the printed negative wording admits two events, so the stem specifies preemptive priority scheduling.

Modified from the original question: the printed negative wording also admitted a higher-priority arrival; the stem now asks which event causes neither blocking nor preemption under preemptive priority scheduling.

An I/O request or waiting for another process blocks the running process until an event completes. A higher-priority arrival preempts it to ready. A lower-priority arrival leaves it running; therefore that event alone causes neither transition.
qs.rel: Under preemptive priority, only a higher-priority arrival or an I/O request affects running process; a lower-priority arrival neither blocks nor preempts. Also consider equal priority.

qs.stem:
Consider the following disk request sequence for a disk with 100 tracks.
 60, 45, 21, 67
 Head pointer starting at 60 and moving in the left direction. Find the number of head movements in cylinders using FCFS scheduling.
qs.sol:
Concept: First Come First Served (FCFS) services disk requests in arrival order. Head movement for one transition is the absolute difference between its starting and destination cylinder. The initial direction does not make the head continue to an edge or wrap around.

Start at 60 and service the request for 60: |60 − 60| = 0 cylinders.

Service 45 next: |60 − 45| = 15 cylinders.

Service 21 next: |45 − 21| = 24 cylinders.

Service 67 last: |21 − 67| = 46 cylinders. The head reverses direction directly; FCFS does not require travel to cylinder 0 or a wrap to the other edge.

Add the four movements: 0 + 15 + 24 + 46 = 85 cylinders.

Cross-check: the request order is 60 → 60 → 45 → 21 → 67. …
qs.rel: FCFS disk head movement = sum of absolute differences in request order. Alternatives: SSTF (nearest), SCAN (elevator), C-SCAN, LOOK. Total seeks measured in cylinders.

qs.stem: Let there be four processes P1, P2, P3, P4 whose CPU burst times are 6, 8, 7, 3 ms, respectively, and they arrive at time 0. Which of the following is the average waiting time and order of the process scheduling under the shortest-job-first scheduling?

opts.A: Average Waiting time = 7.75 ms; Process order: P1, P4, P3, P2
opts.B: Average Waiting time = 7 ms; Process order: P4, P1, P3, P2
opts.C: Average Waiting time = 9.25 ms; Process order: P2, P4, P3, P1
opts.D: Average Waiting time = 10.25 ms; Process order: P1, P2, P3, P4

qs.sol:
In shortest-job-first (SJF) scheduling with non-preemptive execution, whenever every process is already available (arrives at time 0), the scheduler always picks the process with the smallest burst time next; because the order is decided just once at the start, the waiting time of each process equals the sum of the burst times of every process that runs before it, and the average waiting time is the mean of these four waiting times.

The given burst times are P1 = 6 ms, P2 = 8 ms, P3 = 7 ms, P4 = 3 ms; sorting them in ascending order of burst time gives the execution sequence P4 (3 ms) -> P1 (6 ms) -> P3 (7 ms) -> P2 (8 ms).

P4 runs first, so it waits 0 ms. …
qs.rel: Non-preemptive SJF picks shortest burst among arrived jobs. Waiting time = start - arrival; average waiting time for SJF is minimum among non-preemptive algorithms. Compare with FCFS.

qs.stem:
Assume that the following jobs are to be executed on a single processor system. All jobs have arrived at 0 msec.

If the system uses Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling, then calculate the average waiting time of the jobs.
qs.sol:
Using Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling, processes are executed in increasing order of burst time.

Burst times:
b = 1, d = 2, a = 4, c = 7

Execution order:
b → d → a → c

Waiting times:
• b = 0
• d = 1
• a = 1 + 2 = 3
• c = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7

Average waiting time:  7+3+1+0 /4  = 2.75 ms

So, the average waiting time is 2.75 ms.
qs.rel: SJF with all arrivals at 0: sort bursts ascending, waiting times are cumulative sums. Average waiting time is minimal; contrast with FCFS (ordered by arrival) and RR.
